title: Camp 4 close: you've joined the cycle
hook: fourteen portions read closely; the cycle keeps turning, and year two finishes it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Va'era: fire and ice together in the hail. This week, Moses said you can say it, then four cups, tired ears, gratitude even to water, and the finger of God. Today, camp four closes.

Somewhere this week, in a synagogue in Buenos Aires, a teenager is practicing a Torah portion for a bar or bat mitzvah. In Tel Aviv, an old man reads the same portion on the bus. In a kitchen in Ohio, a family argues about it over Friday dinner. In a prison chaplain's office, in a college dorm, in a hospital room: the same few chapters, the same week, all over the world. For the last seventy-five days, at your own pace, you've been reading those chapters too.
screen: `BUENOS AIRES, TEL AVIV, OHIO.` → `THE SAME CHAPTERS, THE SAME WEEK.` → `YOU'VE BEEN DOING IT TOO.`

segments.voice: Camp four was the text: one portion a week. It began with how the Torah is read: a handwritten scroll, heard, not just read. Then fourteen portions, one after another, the way Jews read them. Bereshit, the beginning, and two creation accounts. Noach, and a window in the ark. Lech Lecha: go, and be a blessing. Vayera: shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly? Chayei Sarah: a death portion called life. Toldot: Rebekah asking why. Vayetze: Jacob leaving town. Vayishlach: too small for all this kindness. Vayeshev: wanting to settle. Miketz: it ends suddenly, and Joseph washing his face. Vayigash: Judah drew near. Vayechi: and he lived, and true kindness. Shemot: names, a lamb, holy ground. And Va'era: four cups, and fire in the hail. That's the parashah, the weekly portion, and it never stops. The Torah is divided into fifty-four portions, read in an annual cycle, with some weeks doubling up. On the holiday of Simchat Torah, they read the last lines of Deuteronomy, and then, without a breath, the first lines of Genesis. In the beginning, again. Some congregations follow a three-year cycle instead. Either way, the circle has no finish line. This camp stopped at Va'era. The next portion is Bo, and the plagues continue; you'll pick up the thread in year two. But the cycle doesn't wait. It keeps turning, and you now know how to step into it.
screen: `ONE PORTION A WEEK.` · `FOURTEEN PORTIONS, BERESHIT TO VA'ERA.` · `FIFTY-FOUR PORTIONS, ONE CIRCLE.` · `NEXT COMES BO.` · then, large: `THE CYCLE KEEPS TURNING.`

segments.voice: Let the fourteen portions pass by in your mind: a window, a blessing, a laugh, a ladder, a coat, a cup, wagons, crossed hands, a burning bush, a finger of God. Which one stayed with you? Hold it.
Parashah, the weekly Torah portion, read one at a time in a cycle of fifty-four that circles from Bereshit all the way back to Bereshit again.
Your line: the cycle keeps turning. Tomorrow, camp five: the depths, and the wisdom underneath. Camp four, complete.

howItsDone: Jews read the weekly Torah portion aloud from a scroll on Shabbat morning, with shorter readings on Mondays, Thursdays and Shabbat afternoon; on Simchat Torah the annual cycle ends and immediately begins again with Genesis.

chat.says: Does the weekly Torah reading ever finish, or does it just keep going?
options: It keeps going. On Simchat Torah they read the end, then start Genesis again.
It finishes each fall, and then there's a year off before it starts again.
It ends after fourteen portions, at the burning bush and the plagues.
chat.meaning: The parashah never stops: fifty-four portions in a cycle. On Simchat Torah the last lines of Deuteronomy run straight into Bereshit again.

Simchat Torah.meaning: the holiday when the reading ends and begins again

Hook softened: the learner read fourteen portions in about seventy-five days, not in step with the synagogue calendar, so 'you've been doing it too' became 'at your own pace, you've been reading those chapters too'.

Trapdoor states the annual cycle as Babylonian and the roughly three-year cycle as ancient Land of Israel practice; this is the standard account (Megillah 29b), but the exact origins and length of the triennial cycle are debated by historians. Confirm framing.
